claim: Posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) is implicated in psychiatric and neurological disease.
source: Posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) is an enigmatic region implicated in psychiatric and neurological disease, yet its role in cognition remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to existing literature on PCC's role in disease.

claim: The role of PCC in cognition remains unclear.
source: Posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) is an enigmatic region implicated in psychiatric and neurological disease, yet its role in cognition remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Human studies link PCC to episodic memory and default mode network (DMN).
source: Human studies link PCC to episodic memory and default mode network (DMN), while findings from the non-human primate emphasize executive processes more associated with the cognitive control network (CCN) in humans.
evidence: This claim references existing human studies linking PCC to episodic memory and DMN.

claim: Findings from the non-human primate emphasize executive processes in PCC more associated with the cognitive control network (CCN) in humans.
source: Human studies link PCC to episodic memory and default mode network (DMN), while findings from the non-human primate emphasize executive processes more associated with the cognitive control network (CCN) in humans.
evidence: This claim references existing non-human primate studies showing executive processes in PCC.

claim: The difference between human and non-human primate findings reflects an important functional division between dorsal (executive) and ventral (episodic) PCC.
source: We hypothesized this difference reflects an important functional division between dorsal (executive) and ventral (episodic) PCC.
evidence: This is the authors' hypothesis based on inference from existing literature.

claim: Dorsal PCC population responses were significantly enhanced for executive, compared to episodic, task conditions.
source: Dorsal PCC population responses were significantly enhanced for executive, compared to episodic, task conditions, consistent with the CCN.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Single unit recordings revealed four distinct functional types with unique executive (CCN) or episodic (DMN) response profiles.
source: Single unit recordings, however, revealed four distinct functional types with unique executive (CCN) or episodic (DMN) response profiles.
evidence: This claim is supported by single unit recording data from the study.

claim: PCC remains one of the least understood neocortical areas, with little consensus as to its role in cognition.
source: Despite being routinely observed in studies of human brain function, the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) remains one of the least understood neocortical areas, with little consensus as to its role in cognition (Leech and Sharp, 2014; Leech and Smallwood, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review literature.

claim: PCC reflects the caudal aspect of the cingulate cortex, wrapping around the posterior trunk and splenium of the corpus callosum.
source: Anatomically, PCC reflects the caudal aspect of the cingulate cortex, wrapping around the posterior trunk and splenium of the corpus callosum (Vogt et al., 1995; Vogt et al., 2001; Margulies et al., 2009; Figure 1B).
evidence: This anatomical description is supported by citations and Figure 1B.

claim: PCC displays high basal levels of metabolic activity.
source: Physiologically, PCC displays high basal levels of metabolic activity (Raichle et al., 2001; Buckner et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A growing literature suggests PCC is implicated in the progression of neurodegenerative and psychiatric disease.
source: Clinically, a growing literature suggests PCC is implicated in the progression of neurodegenerative and psychiatric disease (Leech and Sharp, 2014; Vogt, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: The deep medial location and rich vascularization of PCC limit the occurrence of focal insult and corresponding neuropsychological findings.
source: However, the deep medial location and rich vascularization of PCC (Bernier et al., 2018) limit the occurrence of focal insult and corresponding neuropsychological findings, often foundational to understanding many other brain regions (Vaidya et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations regarding PCC anatomy and neuropsychological methods.

claim: Human PCC is typically theorized within its role as a core node of the default mode network (DMN).
source: At present, theorizing on the function of human PCC is typically limited to its role as a core node of the default mode network (DMN) (Raichle et al., 2001; Fox et al., 2005; Fransson, 2005; Fransson and Marrelec, 2008; Buckner and DiNicola, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to DMN literature.

claim: PCC, as part of the DMN, displays high basal levels of activity that are reduced during a variety of tasks, especially those requiring focused attention and cognitive control.
source: Whereby, a large functional neuroimaging literature shows that PCC, as part of the DMN, displays high basal levels of activity that are reduced during a variety of tasks, especially those requiring focused attention and cognitive control (Shulman et al., 1997; Raichle et al., 2001; Harrison et al., 2008; Anticevic et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: The DMN is often reported as being anti-correlated or oppositional to other brain systems, such as the dorsal attention or cognitive control networks (DAN; CCN) that are engaged during attention demanding tasks.
source: Consequently, the DMN is often reported as being anti-correlated or oppositional to other brain systems, such as the dorsal attention or cognitive control networks (DAN; CCN) that are engaged during attention demanding tasks (Fox et al., 2005; Fransson, 2005; Uddin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to network neuroscience literature.

claim: The DMN, and in turn PCC, has been termed 'task-negative', as opposed to 'task-positive' regions.
source: These findings led to the DMN, and in turn PCC, to be termed 'task-negative', as opposed to 'task-positive' regions (Fox et al., 2005; Uddin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature defining task-negative networks.

claim: Hemodynamic activity in PCC is not decreased in all tasks.
source: However, hemodynamic activity in PCC is not decreased in all tasks (Spreng, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: PCC activity increases during episodic memory retrieval.
source: In particular, it increases during episodic memory retrieval (Shannon and Buckner, 2004; Wagner et al., 2005; Vincent et al., 2006) and other internally focused cognitive tasks associated with self-referential thought and envisioning past or future scenarios (Svoboda et al., 2006; Hassabis and Maguire, 2007; Harrison et al., 2008; Spreng et al., 2009; Buckner and DiNicola, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: PCC activity increases during other internally focused cognitive tasks associated with self-referential thought and envisioning past or future scenarios.
source: In particular, it increases during episodic memory retrieval (Shannon and Buckner, 2004; Wagner et al., 2005; Vincent et al., 2006) and other internally focused cognitive tasks associated with self-referential thought and envisioning past or future scenarios (Svoboda et al., 2006; Hassabis and Maguire, 2007; Harrison et al., 2008; Spreng et al., 2009; Buckner and DiNicola, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: PCC/DMN function is associated with 'internally', versus 'externally', focused cognition.
source: These findings highlight an alternate dichotomy where PCC/DMN function is associated with 'internally', versus 'externally', focused cognition (Buckner and Carroll, 2007; Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: Human intracranial recordings of PCC and surrounding posteromedial cortex (PMC) suggest clear electrophysiological evidence of activity suppression during external attention.
source: Supporting these neuroimaging findings, human intracranial recordings of PCC and surrounding posteromedial cortex (PMC) suggest clear electrophysiological evidence of activity suppression during external attention (Miller et al., 2009; Dastjerdi et al., 2011; Ossandón et al., 2011; Foster et al., 2012; Foster et al., 2015) and activity enhancement during cued episodic thought (Foster et al., 2012; Foster et al., 2015; Fox et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to intracranial recording studies.

claim: Human intracranial recordings of PCC and surrounding posteromedial cortex (PMC) suggest activity enhancement during cued episodic thought.
source: Supporting these neuroimaging findings, human intracranial recordings of PCC and surrounding posteromedial cortex (PMC) suggest clear electrophysiological evidence of activity suppression during external attention (Miller et al., 2009; Dastjerdi et al., 2011; Ossandón et al., 2011; Foster et al., 2012; Foster et al., 2015) and activity enhancement during cued episodic thought (Foster et al., 2012; Foster et al., 2015; Fox et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to intracranial recording studies.

claim: Electrophysiological studies in the non-human primate have focused on the contributions of PCC to cognitive control.
source: In contrast, electrophysiological studies in the non-human primate have focused on the contributions of PCC to cognitive control (Hayden et al., 2010), decision making (McCoy et al., 2003; McCoy and Platt, 2005; Pearson et al., 2009), and value judgement (Hayden et al., 2008; Heilbronner et al., 2011) – conditions thought to anti-correlate with PCC engagement in humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to non-human primate studies.

claim: Electrophysiological studies in the non-human primate have focused on the contributions of PCC to decision making.
source: In contrast, electrophysiological studies in the non-human primate have focused on the contributions of PCC to cognitive control (Hayden et al., 2010), decision making (McCoy et al., 2003; McCoy and Platt, 2005; Pearson et al., 2009), and value judgement (Hayden et al., 2008; Heilbronner et al., 2011) – conditions thought to anti-correlate with PCC engagement in humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to non-human primate studies.

claim: Electrophysiological studies in the non-human primate have focused on the contributions of PCC to value judgement.
source: In contrast, electrophysiological studies in the non-human primate have focused on the contributions of PCC to cognitive control (Hayden et al., 2010), decision making (McCoy et al., 2003; McCoy and Platt, 2005; Pearson et al., 2009), and value judgement (Hayden et al., 2008; Heilbronner et al., 2011) – conditions thought to anti-correlate with PCC engagement in humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to non-human primate studies.

claim: Single unit recordings in the macaque PCC during economic decisions have led to a hypothesized role in strategy selection.
source: Together, single unit recordings in the macaque PCC during economic decisions have led to a hypothesized role in strategy selection (Pearson et al., 2009; Pearson et al., 2011; Heilbronner and Platt, 2013), further emphasizing a much more executive function, in apparent contrast to the common focus of human data.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to macaque studies.

claim: Studies of human decision making and value judgements consistently observe PCC engagement.
source: However, studies of human decision making and value judgements consistently observe PCC engagement (Bartra et al., 2013; Clithero and Rangel, 2014; Oldham et al., 2018), yet such findings have received limited attention (compared to anterior cingulate cortex) and therefore limited integration with studies of the DMN (Acikalin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human neuroimaging studies.

claim: Contemporary studies of human brain network organization suggest that PCC contains putative subregions associated with multiple distinct functional systems.
source: Contemporary studies of human brain network organization suggest that PCC contains putative subregions associated with multiple distinct functional systems (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010; Yeo et al., 2011; Leech et al., 2012; Bzdok et al., 2015; Glasser et al., 2016; Braga and Buckner, 2017; Gordon et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to network parcellation studies.

claim: Functional connectivity patterns are consistent with estimated structural connectivity, with prefrontal cingulum tracts entering primarily via the dorsal aspect of PCC, whereas medial temporal lobe tracts enter via its ventral aspect.
source: For example, functional connectivity patterns are consistent with estimated structural connectivity, with prefrontal cingulum tracts entering primarily via the dorsal aspect of PCC, whereas medial temporal lobe tracts enter via its ventral aspect (Greicius et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a connectivity study.

claim: Evidence for PCC subregional organization derives from homologous cytoarchitectural and connectivity data in humans and non-human primates.
source: Evidence for PCC subregional organization also derives from homologous cytoarchitectural and connectivity data in humans and non-human primates (Vogt et al., 1995; Vogt et al., 2001; Vogt and Laureys, 2005; Parvizi et al., 2006; Vogt et al., 2006; Margulies et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Dorsal PCC (dPCC) may be associated with executive control systems of the frontal lobe and ventral PCC (vPCC) may be associated with episodic memory systems of the medial-temporal lobe.
source: Such a division suggests that dorsal PCC (dPCC) may be associated with executive control systems of the frontal lobe and ventral PCC (vPCC) may be associated with episodic memory systems of the medial-temporal lobe (Vincent et al., 2008; Spreng et al., 2010; Leech et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to connectivity studies and represents an inference about functional organization.

claim: Studies in the non-human primate have exclusively focused on the dPCC (often termed area CGp).
source: This subregional perspective better reconciles functional views of PCC across species, as studies in the non-human primate have exclusively focused on the dPCC (often termed area CGp; McCoy et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to non-human primate literature.

claim: Executive attention demanding tasks typically suppress electrophysiological activity within human PCC, consistent with DMN function.
source: As noted above, extant data from humans suggests executive attention demanding tasks typically suppress electrophysiological activity within human PCC, consistent with DMN function (Buckner and DiNicola, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Electrophysiological evidence of PCC engagement during executive tasks, consistent with CCN function, is more limited.
source: In contrast, electrophysiological evidence of PCC engagement during executive tasks, consistent with CCN function, is more limited (Daitch and Parvizi, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an electrophysiology study.

claim: Subregions of PCC, specifically within its dorsal aspect, should be engaged during executive attention demanding tasks more than memory demanding tasks.
source: Based on human neuroimaging and non-human primate electrophysiology, we hypothesized that subregions of PCC, specifically within its dorsal aspect, should be engaged during executive attention demanding tasks more than memory demanding tasks.
evidence: This is the authors' hypothesis based on inference from prior literature.

claim: dPCC should reflect an electrophysiological response profile more consistent with the CCN rather than the DMN.
source: Whereby, dPCC should reflect an electrophysiological response profile more consistent with the CCN rather than the DMN (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is the authors' hypothesis, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Neural populations within dPCC showed significantly greater responses (in broadband gamma, BBG; 70–150 Hz) during executive compared to episodic conditions.
source: We observed that neural populations within dPCC, as captured by the LFP, showed significantly greater responses (in broadband gamma, BBG; 70–150 Hz) during executive compared to episodic conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: A majority of single units responded selectively to only one of the two executive attention tasks (visual search or arithmetic).
source: A majority of single units responded selectively to only one of the two executive attention tasks (visual search or arithmetic), suggesting distinct populations underlie the observed CCN-like LFP response.
evidence: This claim is supported by single unit recording data from the study.

claim: A third functional cell type showed clear selectivity to both episodic memory conditions (past and future event scenarios) as well as suppression to both executive task conditions.
source: However, a third functional cell type showed clear selectivity to both episodic memory conditions (past and future event scenarios) as well as suppression to both executive task conditions, highly consistent with DMN function.
evidence: This claim is supported by single unit recording data from the study.

claim: A final functional cell type displayed increased firing during cued rest periods, also a feature of the DMN.
source: A final functional cell type displayed increased firing during cued rest periods, also a feature of the DMN.
evidence: This claim is supported by single unit recording data from the study.

claim: Electrophysiological activity in PCC was recorded by stereo-electroencephalography (sEEG) depth electrodes in 20 subjects undergoing invasive monitoring for epilepsy.
source: Electrophysiological activity in PCC was recorded by stereo-electroencephalography (sEEG) depth electrodes in 20 subjects undergoing invasive monitoring for epilepsy (female = 8; male = 12; see Methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and subject population.

claim: Across subjects, 35 electrodes were localized to the PCC region, 29 within dPCC and 6 within vPCC.
source: Across subjects, 35 electrodes were localized to the PCC region, 29 within dPCC and 6 within vPCC (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This describes the electrode localization data, shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Task performance showed high accuracy for the executive conditions (mean accuracy: 86.47% for search; 92.59% for add).
source: Task performance showed high accuracy for the executive conditions (mean accuracy: 86.47% for search; 92.59% for add) and robust vividness scores for the cued episodic conditions (modal vividness response: 'strong' for past; 'strong' for future).
evidence: This describes behavioral performance data from the study.

claim: Task performance showed robust vividness scores for the cued episodic conditions (modal vividness response: 'strong' for past; 'strong' for future).
source: Task performance showed high accuracy for the executive conditions (mean accuracy: 86.47% for search; 92.59% for add) and robust vividness scores for the cued episodic conditions (modal vividness response: 'strong' for past; 'strong' for future).
evidence: This describes behavioral performance data from the study.

claim: BBG activity is strongly correlated with both blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) fMRI and population firing rate.
source: BBG activity is strongly correlated with both blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) fMRI and population firing rate, making it a useful marker for reconciling human neuroimaging and non-human primate electrophysiology findings (Miller, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on BBG.

claim: dPCC displayed increased activity specifically within the BBG range during the cue and early task execution of the executive attention conditions, search and add.
source: We found that dPCC displayed increased activity specifically within the BBG range during the cue and early task execution of the executive attention conditions, search and add.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Group data shows BBG activation within dPCC to be transient and peaked following the onset of search and add tasks.
source: Group data (nprobes = 29, nsubjects = 19) shows BBG activation within dPCC to be transient and peaked following the onset of search and add tasks (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by group-level data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: During early task execution, from task onset to 1000 ms, group mean BBG amplitude was greatest for the search condition, followed by the add condition, with low mean responses for past, future, and rest conditions.
source: During early task execution, from task onset to 1000 ms (1000–2000 ms post-cue), group mean BBG amplitude was greatest for the search condition, followed by the add condition, with low mean responses for past, future, and rest conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Mean BBG amplitude was significantly higher for the search task compared to add, past, future, and rest conditions.
source: Specifically, mean BBG amplitude was significantly higher for the search task compared to add, past, future, and rest conditions (search-add: t(5093)=3.859, p=0.0011; search-past: t(5093)=8.092, p<0.0001; search-future: t(5093)=8.573, p<0.0001; search-rest: t(5093)=8.706, p<0.0001), and furthermore, was significantly higher for the add task compared to past, future, and rest conditions (add-past: t(5093)=4.236, p=0.0002; add-future: t(5093)=4.717, p<0.0001; add-rest: t(5093)=4.847, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Mean BBG amplitude was significantly higher for the add task compared to past, future, and rest conditions.
source: Specifically, mean BBG amplitude was significantly higher for the search task compared to add, past, future, and rest conditions (search-add: t(5093)=3.859, p=0.0011; search-past: t(5093)=8.092, p<0.0001; search-future: t(5093)=8.573, p<0.0001; search-rest: t(5093)=8.706, p<0.0001), and furthermore, was significantly higher for the add task compared to past, future, and rest conditions (add-past: t(5093)=4.236, p=0.0002; add-future: t(5093)=4.717, p<0.0001; add-rest: t(5093)=4.847, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Sites within vPCC showed the converse BBG response profile across conditions, consistent with the DMN and prior observations.
source: In contrast, sites within vPCC (nprobes = 6) showed the converse BBG response profile across conditions, consistent with the DMN and prior observations (Dastjerdi et al., 2011; Foster et al., 2012; Foster et al., 2015), where BBG responses were greater during late task execution (2000–3000 ms after task onset) for the episodic task conditions (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior studies.

claim: vPCC mean BBG amplitude was significantly higher for past than all other conditions.
source: A mixed effects model revealed a significant main effect of condition on BBG amplitude, with vPCC mean BBG amplitude being significantly higher for past than all other conditions (past-add: t(1253)=8.841, p<0.0001; past-search: t(1253)=5.151, p<0.0001; past-rest: t(1253)=3.978, p=0.0007; past-future: t(1253)=3.020, p=0.0216), and significantly lower for add than all other conditions (add-past: t(1253)=–8.841, p<0.0001; add-future: t(1253)=–5.811, p<0.0001; add-rest: t(1253)=–4.863, p<0.0001; add-search: t(1253)=–3.690, p=0.0022).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: vPCC mean BBG amplitude was significantly lower for add than all other conditions.
source: A mixed effects model revealed a significant main effect of condition on BBG amplitude, with vPCC mean BBG amplitude being significantly higher for past than all other conditions (past-add: t(1253)=8.841, p<0.0001; past-search: t(1253)=5.151, p<0.0001; past-rest: t(1253)=3.978, p=0.0007; past-future: t(1253)=3.020, p=0.0216), and significantly lower for add than all other conditions (add-past: t(1253)=–8.841, p<0.0001; add-future: t(1253)=–5.811, p<0.0001; add-rest: t(1253)=–4.863, p<0.0001; add-search: t(1253)=–3.690, p=0.0022).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Executive activity during an early time window (task onset to 1 s) was maximal for sites closer to the callosal sulcus within dPCC (i.e. inferior aspect of dPCC).
source: As shown in Figure 3A, executive activity during an early time window (task onset to 1 s) was maximal for sites closer to the callosal sulcus within dPCC (i.e. inferior aspect of dPCC).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis of electrode data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When considering a later time period of task execution, 2–3 s after task onset, population selectivity appeared to follow a more dorsal/ventral gradient with executive activity more dorsal and mnemonic activity more ventral within PCC.
source: When considering a later time period of task execution, 2–3 s after task onset, population selectivity appeared to follow a more dorsal/ventral gradient with executive activity more dorsal and mnemonic activity more ventral within PCC (Figure 3C/D).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis of electrode data shown in Figure 3C/D.

claim: Meta-analytic association of neuroimaging studies for the term 'cognitive control' identifies commonly reported activations within the inferior aspect of dPCC.
source: Indeed, meta-analytic association of neuroimaging studies for the term 'cognitive control' identifies commonly reported activations within the inferior aspect of dPCC (Neurosynth association test; n studies = 598).
evidence: This claim is supported by meta-analysis of neuroimaging data.

claim: Microwires extending from the distal tip of a subset of sEEG probes allowed for recording, detecting, and sorting single unit spiking activity within dPCC (nprobes = 6; nunits = 91).
source: Microwires extending from the distal tip of a subset of sEEG probes allowed for recording, detecting, and sorting single unit spiking activity within dPCC (nprobes = 6; nunits = 91; See Methods).
evidence: This describes the single unit recording methods and sample size.

claim: PCC neurons varied in their mean firing rate, but predominately displayed sparse firing properties, with a group mean spike rate of 1.7 Hz.
source: Overall, PCC neurons varied in their mean firing rate, but predominately displayed sparse firing properties, with a group mean spike rate of 1.7 Hz (across entire task).
evidence: This claim is supported by single unit recording data from the study.

claim: Unsupervised hierarchical clustering of units based on the similarity of task response profiles identified four putative functional types.
source: Therefore, we applied unsupervised hierarchical clustering of units based on the similarity of task response profiles to identify putative functional types (See Methods; Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Strikingly, this clustering revealed four clear functional types, with several unique response features.
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis of single unit data, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Type 1 units (nunits = 13) were selective for the search condition only.
source: These two functional types showed condition-specific selectivity within the executive tasks, where Type 1 (nunits = 13) was selective for the search condition only, whereas Type 2 (nunits = 34) was selective for the add condition only.
evidence: This claim is supported by single unit recording data from the study.

claim: Type 2 units (nunits = 34) were selective for the add condition only.
source: These two functional types showed condition-specific selectivity within the executive tasks, where Type 1 (nunits = 13) was selective for the search condition only, whereas Type 2 (nunits = 34) was selective for the add condition only.
evidence: This claim is supported by single unit recording data from the study.

claim: Type 1 and 2 units showed increased activity beginning during the cue period and continuing to increase with task engagement.
source: Similar to LFP BBG responses, Type 1 and 2 units showed increased activity beginning during the cue period and continuing to increase with task engagement.
evidence: This claim is supported by single unit recording data from the study.

claim: Type 3 units (nunits = 26) displayed firing rates that were increased for both the past and future episodic conditions, weakly elevated for the rest condition, and suppressed for both executive task conditions (search/add).
source: Whereby, Type 3 units (nunits = 26), displayed firing rates that were increased for both the past and future episodic conditions, weakly elevated for the rest condition, and suppressed for both executive task conditions (search/add; Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Type 3 units showed a more delayed increase in firing rate, occurring well after the start of task engagement.
source: Furthermore, unlike Type 1 and 2 units, Type 3 units showed a more delayed increase in firing rate, occurring well after the start of task engagement.
evidence: This claim is supported by single unit recording data from the study.

claim: Type 4 units (nunits = 18) primarily displayed increased firing rates to the rest condition.
source: Finally, Type 4 units (nunits = 18) primarily displayed increased firing rates to the rest condition, which is another related functional property often associated with the DMN (Dastjerdi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by single unit recording data and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Type 4 units, which typically showed higher basal firing rates, increased firing after the cue was presented.
source: These units, which typically showed higher basal firing rates, increased firing after the cue was presented.
evidence: This claim is supported by single unit recording data from the study.

claim: There was initially no significant main effect of task condition on firing rate (p=0.55) prior to considering cluster type.
source: Consistent with our observations, there was initially no significant main effect of task condition on firing rate (p=0.55) prior to considering cluster type.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of single unit data.

claim: There was a significant effect of cluster type on mean task firing rate (p=0.01).
source: There was, however, a significant effect of cluster type on mean task firing rate (p=0.01) and a significant interaction between task condition and cluster type (p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of single unit data.

claim: There was a significant interaction between task condition and cluster type (p<0.0001).
source: There was, however, a significant effect of cluster type on mean task firing rate (p=0.01) and a significant interaction between task condition and cluster type (p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of single unit data.

claim: Hierarchical clustering through a complete leave-one-out process resulted in a 94% identical cluster rate.
source: To quantify the consistency of cluster membership, we performed hierarchical clustering through a complete leave-one-out process, resulting in a 94% identical cluster rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by validation analysis of the clustering approach.

claim: Each of the four functional cell types were observed on multiple microwire probes, indicating that none of the cluster types originated from a single subject or recording site.
source: Importantly, each of the four functional cell types were observed on multiple microwire probes, indicating that none of the cluster types originated from a single subject or recording site.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the distribution of cell types across recording sites.

claim: Each microwire probe gave rise to units of different selectivity types, suggesting a more mixed organization at the single unit level.
source: Furthermore, each microwire probe gave rise to units of different selectivity types, suggesting a more mixed organization at the single unit level.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the distribution of cell types across recording sites.

claim: Intracranial recordings targeting human dPCC revealed strong electrophysiological evidence of executive task engagement.
source: Intracranial recordings targeting human dPCC revealed strong electrophysiological evidence of executive task engagement.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Dorsal PCC neural populations displayed executive processing activity profiles consistent with that of cognitive control regions, as opposed to the episodic/DMN activity commonly attributed to the entire PCC.
source: Dorsal PCC neural populations, as captured by LFP broadband gamma activity, displayed executive processing activity profiles consistent with that of cognitive control regions, as opposed to the episodic/DMN activity commonly attributed to the entire PCC (Fox et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the experimental data and contrasted with prior literature.

claim: Across-subject consideration of the spatial organization of population responses showed some clustering of executive selectivity inferior within dPCC near the callosal sulcus.
source: Across-subject consideration of the spatial organization of population responses showed some clustering of executive selectivity inferior within dPCC near the callosal sulcus.
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis of electrode data.

claim: Neurons in dPCC exhibited distinct selectivity profiles for specific executive attention tasks (search or add), consistent with, but more selective than, LFP data.
source: Neurons in dPCC exhibited distinct selectivity profiles for specific executive attention tasks (search or add), consistent with, but more selective than, LFP data.
evidence: This claim is supported by single unit recording data from the study.

claim: A distinct set of neurons showed a clear DMN type of functional profile selective to either episodic processing (past and future) conditions or rest periods.
